ai.title: Track changes already applied during tool execution
ai.summary: Renamed `previousChanges` to `changesAlreadyApplied` in WebSocket schemas and propagated it through backend handlers and CLI clients. This ensures the client accumulates all file modifications made before and during tool calls, displaying a complete diff at the end of the request. Updated `common/src/actions.ts`, `backend/src/main-prompt.ts`, and `npm-app/src/cli.ts` to merge `changesAlreadyApplied` with new changes for accurate state tracking.

eli5.text: When you ask the assistant to edit your files, the final summary now shows the complete list of every file that changed during that conversation, including edits made before any tools ran alongside the ones made by the tools themselves. This affects anyone who uses the assistant to modify code, and you'll notice a more complete diff at the end instead of seeing only the most recent changes.

eli5.text: The behind-the-scenes instructions that guide how the assistant works have been quietly updated to include a new step: after making any change, it should double-check its work by running tests or other verification tools, similar to proofreading before sending an email. This doesn't change anything you see, but makes sure future edits are less likely to break things. It's already in effect today.

This is a behind-the-scenes housekeeping update that keeps the app's version number in sync with changes already released. The version label itself does nothing new, but the batch of fixes and improvements now packaged under this number includes correcting a crash when processing certain code edits, tracking which edits have already been applied, and adding a step that checks changes before they are finalized. Nothing about what you can install or run today changed because of the label alone; this just keeps everyone's installations current with the fixes already in play.

Previously, the instructions just said to run a type checker after changes; now they require running it after every single change and fixing any type errors that come up. This affects anyone who contributes code to the project, when you make a change, you’ll now need to follow a stricter check before it’s considered done. If you looked, you’d see the guidance section renamed and the wording tightened, but the app itself works exactly the same as before.

eli5.text: When a message sent to the chat can't be read as proper text, the system now logs that error in a cleaner layout so developers can spot the problem faster, but the actual error reporting and recovery steps it takes stayed exactly the same. Behind the scenes, one internal component that tracks stale chat sessions was given a more flexible type so the code could compile and load correctly. This is housekeeping for the engineering team, not something you'd see change in the app today. If you looked, you'd only notice tidier formatting in the error logs when unreadable messages arrive; everything else in how the chat reacts behaves as before.

ai.title: Preserve whitespace in parsed diff blocks
ai.summary: Removed `removeNewlinesFromStartAndEnd` helper from `backend/src/generate-diffs-prompt.ts`. `parseAndGetDiffBlocks` and `parseAndGetDiffBlocksSingleFile` now preserve leading/trailing newlines in `searchContent` and `replaceContent` to ensure exact matching. Updated `backend/knowledge.md` with whitespace handling rules for search/replace blocks.

eli5.text: The assistant can now follow instructions that include blank lines at the start or end of text blocks without accidentally removing them, which means exact-match edits are more reliable when your code has spacing around changes. Previously, any leading or trailing blank lines in a section to search for or replace were stripped away before matching, so edits that relied on that exact spacing could fail silently. This only affects how the system handles internal edit instructions, so you wouldn't notice it directly, but edits are less likely to miss their target due to whitespace.

It's a behind-the-scenes adjustment to a single image file, with no effect on how the site works otherwise. You'd only notice it if you shared a link and saw the preview image that pops up next to it.
